title: How Crew-13 reached the space station in under 8 hours

news_hook.event: NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 (Crew Dragon 'Grace', Falcon 9) launched Oct 1 2026 at 11:10 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40, Cape Canaveral, and docked autonomously to the Harmony module's forward port at 7:05 p.m. EDT: 7 h 55 min launch-to-docking, called the fastest launch-to-docking of a U.S. spacecraft in ISS history.

original_contribution: A step-by-step visual explanation of the counterintuitive core (speeding up makes you fall behind; dropping lower lets you catch up), built from sourced orbital-mechanics facts, with NASA's own wording on the record claim instead of the usual overstatement.

mechanism.step: An orbit is falling around Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it
A forward burn swings you into a wider loop; wider loops take longer, so the target pulls ahead
Braking (firing backward) drops you lower, where gravity is stronger: faster, shorter laps
Phasing: the shorter lap gains a few degrees on the target each time around
The gap is an angle; gap divided by degrees gained per lap = laps needed
Launch time sets the gap: the station's orbit must sweep over the launch site; smaller gap, fewer laps
A short burn climbs you back to the station's orbit; pause at checkpoints; dock autonomously

claims.claim: Crew-13 launched Oct 1 2026 at 11:10 a.m. EDT
Crew-13 docked at 7:05 p.m. EDT (7 h 55 min); NASA calls it the fastest launch-to-docking of a U.S. spacecraft in ISS history
The station travels about 4.8 miles per second (NASA rounds to five; 7.67 km/s)
Lower circular orbits are faster with shorter periods; speeding up gives a higher orbit
Phasing: a different-period orbit turns the angle between spacecraft into time
A drop of ~96.6 km (60 miles) saves ~118 s per lap and gains ~7.8 degrees per lap (computed from circular-orbit formulas, independently recomputed by the fact-check agent)
Rendezvous needs the same orbital plane; launch windows are critical
A Dragon program official said the station was in a good/opportune spot (SECONDARY source; title and exact wording unverified against a NASA transcript)
Staged approach with checkpoints, final approach a few cm/s, Dragon docks autonomously

packaging.description:
On October 1, SpaceX Crew-13 launched at 11:10 a.m. EDT and docked with the space station at 7:05 that night, a U.S. record. Here is how a spacecraft actually catches something moving almost five miles a second.

The surprise: speeding up makes you fall behind. Braking into a lower orbit, where you move faster, is what lets you catch up. NASA hasn't detailed Crew-13's exact burns, so this is the standard method, shown with a worked example.

Sources:

scenes.narration: A SpaceX Dragon capsule left Florida at 11:10 a.m. and reached the space station by 7:05 that night. How?

visual.label: Crew-13, Oct 1. Crew Dragon's first crewed flight (2020) took about 19 h

scenes.narration: The station is already up there, far ahead on the circle, moving almost five miles every second. How do you catch it?

reveal.caption: You start far behind it, on the same orbit

scenes.narration: What is an orbit? Throw a ball sideways fast enough, and the ground curves away before it lands.

reveal.caption: Throw it sideways from a mountain
An orbit: falling, but always missing

scenes.narration: Here is the catch. Burn forward, and you swing out into a wider loop. Wider loops take longer, so the station pulls ahead.
So do the opposite: fire backward to brake. You sink lower, where gravity is stronger, and speed up. Each lap is shorter.
Drop about 60 miles and you gain almost eight degrees a lap, a slice of the 360-degree circle. Engineers call this phasing.

reveal.caption: PHASING: closing the gap, lap by lap

scenes.narration: The gap is the angle between you and the station. Say it is 40 degrees. At eight degrees a lap, that is five laps: about seven and a half hours.

visual.label: each lap ≈ 90 min · a worked example, not Crew-13's actual numbers

scenes.narration: Launch time sets the gap. Liftoff waits until the station's orbit sweeps over Florida. A smaller gap means fewer laps.

reveal.caption: Earth turns under the station's orbit
